title: Where the chain settles
objectives: Find a stationary distribution by solving $\pi P = \pi$.
Read $\pi$ as the long-run share of time in each state.

options.text: Both to about 0.667, whatever the start
Both to 0.5: bull and bear even out

screens.title: A split that does not move
screens.prose: Suppose today is bull with chance $\tfrac23$ and bear with chance $\tfrac13$. Write this as the row vector $\pi = (\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$. Tomorrow's chances are $\pi P$: each entry weights one column of $P$ by today's chances.
screens.question: Fill in tomorrow's chances, as decimals.

hints.text: Bull tomorrow can follow a bull day or a bear day.
Use the bull column of $P$: 0.9 from bull and 0.2 from bear.
Bull: $\tfrac23 \times 0.9 + \tfrac13 \times 0.2 = 0.6 + 0.0667$. Bear: $\tfrac23 \times 0.1 + \tfrac13 \times 0.8$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each column of $P$ by today's chances, then add.

byKey.r0c1: Check the bull entry: $\tfrac23 \times 0.9 + \tfrac13 \times 0.2$. It uses the first column of $P$, not the first row.
byKey.r1c1: Check the bear entry: $\tfrac23 \times 0.1 + \tfrac13 \times 0.8$. It uses the second column of $P$.

explain.text: One step leaves $(\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$ where it was. A distribution with $\pi P = \pi$ is called **stationary**. It is where both bars settled on the last screen.

screens.title: Solve for it
screens.prose: A trading signal is on or off each day. On stays on with chance 0.95; off stays off with chance 0.85. Write $\pi = (x, 1 - x)$, with $x$ the long-run chance the signal is on.

state.caption: Rows and columns in the order on, off.

screens.question: Solve the first column of $\pi P = \pi$: $0.95x + 0.15(1 - x) = x$. What is $x$?

widget.label: Long-run chance the signal is on

hints.text: Collect the $x$ terms on one side.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand $0.15(1 - x)$, then collect the $x$ terms.

byKey.half: You split the time evenly. The signal leaves on less often than it leaves off, so it is on more than half the time.
byKey.swap: 0.25 is the share of days off. You solved for $1 - x$.
byKey.ratio: 3 is the ratio of on days to off days. Writing $\pi = (x, 1 - x)$ makes the shares add to 1, so $x = \tfrac34$.
byKey.diag: 0.95 is the one-day chance that on stays on. The long-run share also counts days that start off.

explain.text: Flow out of on is $0.05x$, and flow into on is $0.15(1 - x)$. They balance at $x = 0.75$. Check: $0.95 \times 0.75 + 0.15 \times 0.25 = 0.75$.

screens.title: Three states by elimination
screens.prose: Write $\pi = (\pi_L, \pi_M, \pi_H)$ for this chain. Column L of $\pi P = \pi$ says $0.75\pi_L + 0.10\pi_M = \pi_L$. Column H says $0.15\pi_M + 0.75\pi_H = \pi_H$.

state.caption: Weekly volatility: low (L), medium (M), high (H). Rows and columns in that order.

screens.question: Eliminate down to $\pi_L$, then fill in the table.

hints.text: Column L gives $0.10\pi_M = 0.25\pi_L$.
Column H gives $0.25\pi_H = 0.15\pi_M$, so $\pi_H = 0.6\pi_M$.
$\pi_M = 2.5\pi_L$ and $\pi_H = 0.6 \times 2.5\pi_L = 1.5\pi_L$. Then $5\pi_L = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\pi_M$ and $\pi_H$ in terms of $\pi_L$, then make the three add to 1.

explain.text: Columns L and H each tie two shares together, and the shares adding to 1 fixes the scale. So $\pi = (0.2, 0.5, 0.3)$. Column M then holds by itself: $0.05 + 0.375 + 0.075 = 0.5$.

screens.title: A state you never leave
screens.prose: A loan is performing (Perf) or in default (Def). Each year a performing loan defaults with chance 0.03. A defaulted loan stays defaulted. Slide the years and watch where the probability goes.
screens.question: What is the stationary distribution $(\pi_{\text{Perf}}, \pi_{\text{Def}})$?

options.why: You read the performing row as the long-run split. That row is one year's move from Perf.
You split evenly between the states. Default is never left, so it collects everything.
You took absorption as the chain stopping. It sits in Def for ever, and $(0, 1)P = (0, 1)$.

hints.text: Slide the years to 100. Where is the probability?
Column Perf of $\pi P = \pi$ reads $0.97\pi_{\text{Perf}} = \pi_{\text{Perf}}$.
That forces $\pi_{\text{Perf}} = 0$, and the shares add to 1.

feedback.correct: All the probability ends in the absorbing state.

explain.text: $0.97\pi_{\text{Perf}} = \pi_{\text{Perf}}$ holds only when $\pi_{\text{Perf}} = 0$. So $\pi = (0, 1)$: Default is the only closed class, and it takes all the long-run mass. After 100 years only $0.97^{100} \approx 0.048$ is still performing.

screens.title: Rows, not columns
screens.prose: A colleague codes the volatility chain. Her code finds $\mathbf{v}$ with $P\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$, as in the eigenvalue course, then scales it to add to 1. It reports $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$.

state.caption: Rows and columns in the order L, M, H. Each row adds to 1.

screens.question: What is the long-run share of high-volatility weeks?

options.why: You trusted $P\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$. Each row of $P$ adds to 1, so $(1, 1, 1)$ solves it for every chain.
That is $1/\sqrt{3}$, a length-1 scaling of her vector. Shares add to 1, and her equation is the wrong one.
0.75 is the chance high stays high for one week. The long run also counts weeks that start low or medium.

hints.text: Do the rows or the columns of $P$ add to 1?
Rows add to 1, so the distribution multiplies $P$ from the left: $\pi P = \pi$.
You solved $\pi P = \pi$ for this chain by elimination two screens ago.

feedback.correct: $\pi = (0.2, 0.5, 0.3)$, so 30% of weeks are high volatility.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The long-run split solves $\pi P = \pi$, with $\pi$ on the left.

byKey.col: You solved $P\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$, the column convention. Here rows add to 1, so the long-run split solves $\pi P = \pi$.

explain.text: With rows adding to 1, $P(1, 1, 1)^T = (1, 1, 1)^T$ for every chain, so her answer says nothing. The eigenvalue course had columns adding to 1, where $M\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}$ was right. Here we need $\pi P = \pi$, which gives 0.3.

screens.title: Any two-state chain
screens.prose: Generalise the signal calculation. Take $P = \begin{pmatrix}1-a & a\\ b & 1-b\end{pmatrix}$ with $a + b > 0$. We need $\pi P = \pi$ and the **normalising equation** $\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 1$. Without it, any multiple of $\pi$ also solves $\pi P = \pi$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\pi_1 = (1 - a)\pi_1 + b\pi_2$, the first column of $\pi P = \pi$
$a\pi_1 = b\pi_2$, subtract $(1 - a)\pi_1$: flow out of state 1 equals flow in
$\pi_1 = \dfrac{b}{a + b}$ and $\pi_2 = \dfrac{a}{a + b}$, divide by $a + b > 0$

hints.text: Start from one column of $\pi P = \pi$.
Next, simplify it into a balance of flows.
Column, balance, normalise, collect, divide.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the column equation, and use the normalising equation only once it is simplified.

byKey.o2: The balance of flows comes from simplifying a column equation, so that equation must come first.
byKey.o3: Substituting $\pi_2 = 1 - \pi_1$ needs the simplified balance $a\pi_1 = b\pi_2$ first.
byKey.o4: Collecting terms needs the line with $\pi_2$ already replaced.
byKey.o5: Dividing by $a + b$ is the last step.

explain.text: Both columns of $\pi P = \pi$ give the same equation, $a\pi_1 = b\pi_2$. The normalising equation supplies the missing one. For the regime chain, $a = 0.1$ and $b = 0.2$, so $\pi_1 = \tfrac{0.2}{0.3} = \tfrac23$.

widget.solution:
import random

P = [[0.9, 0.1],    # from bull
     [0.2, 0.8]]    # from bear

def share_in_bull(days, seed):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    state = 1                  # 0 is bull, 1 is bear
    bull_days = 0
    for _ in range(days):
        if rng.random() < P[state][0]:
            state = 0          # bull next
        else:
            state = 1          # bear next
        bull_days += (state == 0)
    return bull_days / days
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. Over 200,000 days each share must be within 0.015 of $\tfrac23$, and two short runs must match exactly.

hints.text: What should be added on a bull day, and what on a bear day?
After the `if`, `state` is 0 on a bull day.
Add `(state == 0)`: Python counts `True` as 1 and `False` as 0.

feedback.correct: Each bull day adds 1, each bear day adds 0.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Add 1 to `bull_days` exactly when the new state is bull.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that `...` is replaced by an expression.

explain.text:
`bull_days += (state == 0)` adds 1 on a bull day and 0 otherwise. With seeds 1, 2 and 7 the shares are 0.666255, 0.668935 and 0.66784. They converge to exactly $\tfrac23$, the stationary chance of bull.

```python
bull_days += (state == 0)   # True counts as 1
```

screens.title: The long-run average return
screens.prose: Treat each step of the regime chain as one month. A bull month returns 2% on average and a bear month loses 3%. Over many months, each regime counts in proportion to its share of time: the average is $\sum_i \pi_i \mu_i$.
screens.question: What is the long-run average monthly return? Give a percentage.

hints.text: Weight each regime's mean by its long-run share.
The weights are $\pi = (\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each mean by its long-run share, then add.

byKey.simple: You averaged the two returns equally. Bull months are twice as common as bear months.
byKey.diag: You weighted by 0.9 and 0.1, the bull row of $P$. The weights are the long-run shares, $\tfrac23$ and $\tfrac13$.
byKey.swapped: You gave bear the weight $\tfrac23$. Bull is the regime with share $\tfrac23$.

explain.text: Each month's mean depends only on its regime, and $\pi$ says how often each regime occurs. So the long-run mean is $\tfrac23(0.02) + \tfrac13(-0.03) \approx 0.0033$, about 0.33% a month. The bear months cost a lot, but they are only a third of the time.

ideas: A stationary distribution is not moved by a step: $\pi P = \pi$, with $\pi$ a row vector because the rows of $P$ add to 1.
The equations of $\pi P = \pi$ are dependent. Add the normalising equation $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$, then solve by elimination.
The regime chain settles at $\pi$ from any start. And $\pi_i$ is the long-run share of time in state $i$.

formula.name: Stationary distribution
formula.note: Two states: $\pi_1 = \dfrac{b}{a + b}$, where $a = P_{12}$ and $b = P_{21}$.

summary.trap: Solving $P\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}$ uses columns. When rows add to 1, the all-equal vector solves it for every chain.

quiz.prose: A stock trends or ranges each day. $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.6 & 0.4\\ 0.2 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$, rows and columns in the order trending, ranging.
quiz.question: What is the long-run chance the stock is trending?

options.why: 0.6 is the one-day chance that trending stays trending, not a long-run share.
You used $a/(a + b)$. The share of state 1 is $b/(a + b) = 0.2/0.6$.
You split the days evenly. Ranging is stickier, so it gets more of the time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Balance the flows: $0.4\pi_1 = 0.2\pi_2$.

explain.text: Flow out of trending is $0.4\pi_1$ and flow in is $0.2\pi_2$. With $\pi_1 + \pi_2 = 1$, $\pi_1 = \tfrac{0.2}{0.6} = \tfrac13$. Check: $\tfrac13 \times 0.6 + \tfrac23 \times 0.2 = \tfrac13$.

quiz.prose: The regime chain has $P = \begin{pmatrix}0.9 & 0.1\\ 0.2 & 0.8\end{pmatrix}$. Today is bull or bear with chance $\tfrac12$ each.
quiz.question: What is the chance of bull tomorrow?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the bull column, 0.9 and 0.2, by $\tfrac12$ each.

byKey.same: You assumed the split stays put. Only the stationary split does that, and $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ is not it.
byKey.bear: 0.45 is the chance of bear tomorrow. You used the bear column.

explain.text: $\tfrac12 \times 0.9 + \tfrac12 \times 0.2 = 0.55$. The split moved, so $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$ is not stationary. Each step pulls it towards $(\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$.

quiz.prose: A bank's £200m loan book is rated A or B. Each year an A loan stays A with chance 0.9; a B loan moves up to A with chance 0.3. Ignore defaults and repayments.
quiz.question: In the long run, how many millions of pounds of the book are rated A?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $\pi_A$ with $a = 0.1$ and $b = 0.3$, then scale by 200.

byKey.even: You split the book evenly. Loans leave A less often than they leave B.
byKey.diag: You used 0.9, the chance an A loan stays A. The long-run share is $0.3/(0.1 + 0.3)$.
byKey.swap: £50m is the B part of the book. You used $a/(a + b)$.

explain.text: Downgrades are $0.1\pi_A$ and upgrades are $0.3\pi_B$, so $\pi_A = 3\pi_B$ and $\pi_A = 0.75$. Three quarters of £200m is £150m. The mix holds even as single loans move between ratings.

quiz.prose: For the regime chain, both columns of $\pi P = \pi$ reduce to $0.1\pi_1 = 0.2\pi_2$. A student says this has infinitely many solutions, so there is no single long-run split.
quiz.question: Which reply is right?

options.text: The student is right: the long-run split is not unique
options.why: You stopped at $\pi P = \pi$. Probabilities must add to 1, which picks one solution.
That solves $\pi P = \pi$ but adds to 3. Divide by 3 to get probabilities.
You read the coefficients off the equation. $(0.2, 0.1)$ solves $\pi P = \pi$ but adds to 0.3, so it is not a distribution.

feedback.correct: The normalising equation picks the one solution that adds to 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which solutions are probability distributions.

explain.text: Every multiple of $(2, 1)$ solves $\pi P = \pi$, so that system alone is singular. The extra fact that probabilities add to 1 picks out $(\tfrac23, \tfrac13)$. Always pair $\pi P = \pi$ with $\sum_i \pi_i = 1$.
